extracted.intended_audience: travellers and readers wishing to appreciate Gothic cathedrals (specifically Amiens) and ecclesiastical sculpture/architecture
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and aesthetic guidance for approaching, entering, reading, and judging the architecture and sculpture of a Gothic cathedral (with concrete route recommendations, behavioral etiquette, and notes on restoration and workmanship).

rubrics_metrics.name: Approach on foot from the chalk hill to understand height & relation
rubrics_metrics.description: If you have plenty of leisure, and the day is fine ... the really right thing to do is to walk down the main street of the old town, and across the river, and quite out to the chalk hill out of which the citadel is half quarried--half walled;--and walk to the top of that, and look down into the citadel's dry 'ditch' ... and thence across to the cathedral and ascending slopes of the city; so, you will understand the real height and relation of tower and town.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This long walk gives the true sense of the cathedral's scale and its relation to town and landscape; after this, return by narrow winding streets and chance bridges (the more winding and dirty the streets, the better) to increase the pleasure of discovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Short/poor-weather route and mood-setting
rubrics_metrics.description: But if the day be dismal ... or if you must really go to Paris this afternoon, and only mean to see all you can in an hour or two ... I think the best way is to walk from the Hotel de France or the Place de Perigord, up the Street of Three Pebbles, towards the railway station -- stopping a little as you go, so as to get into a cheerful temper, and buying some bonbons or tarts for the children in one of the charming patissiers' shops on the left.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical short route which still preserves a pleasant state of mind for viewing; small acts (buying sweets) prepare a cheerful temper for appreciation. The recommended path leads to the south transept, which 'has really something about it to please everybody.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Give alms graciously when asked
rubrics_metrics.description: Put a sou into every beggar's box who asks it there,--it is none of your business whether they should be there or not, nor whether they deserve to have the sou,--be sure only that you yourself deserve to have it to give; and give it prettily, and not as if it burnt your fingers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Etiquette guidance: give with the right spirit (not grudgingly); behaving kindly is part of the right approach to the sacred place.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enter by the south transept and take an initial 'first sensation' glimpse
rubrics_metrics.description: You cannot enter it to better advantage than by this door ... go in at this south transept door, ... Then, being once inside, take what first sensation and general glimpse of it pleases you--promising the custode to come back to see it properly; (only then mind you keep the promise;) and in this first quarter of an hour, seeing only what fancy bid you--but at least ... the apse from mid-nave, and all the traverses of the building, from its centre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not immediately attempt exhaustive examination. Allow an initial emotional/imaginative response; later return for detailed study as promised to the custode. Focus first on apse-from-mid-nave to perceive what the architect intended.

rubrics_metrics.name: See the inside before judging the outside; use outside to understand interior function
rubrics_metrics.description: Then you will know, when you go outside again, what the architect was working for, and what his buttresses and traceries mean. For the outside of a French cathedral, except for its sculpture, is always to be thought of as the wrong side of the stuff, in which you find how the threads go that produce the inside or right-side pattern.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the exterior as a diagram of structural/functional causes; judge the cathedral primarily by its interior effect (light, space, procession of windows).

rubrics_metrics.name: Spiritual/readiness prerequisite to full appreciation
rubrics_metrics.description: And having prayed this prayer, or at least, read it with honest wishing, (which if you cannot, there is no hope of your at present taking pleasure in any human work of large faculty, whether poetry, painting, or sculpture,) we may walk a little farther ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ruskin argues that a devotional or reflective frame of mind (exemplified by the supplied prayer) is necessary to take pleasure in great works of art; lacking this, the visitor will not fully appreciate monumental art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standardize compass/orientation language and viewpoint
rubrics_metrics.description: You will find it always well, in looking at any cathedral, to make your quarters of the compass sure, in the beginning; ... I shall endeavour in all my future writing of architecture, to observe the simple law of always calling the door of the north transept the north door; and that on the same side of the west front, the northern door, and so of their opposites.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use consistent terminology (north/south/central doors) and define 'right' and 'left' as when going out of the cathedral (walking down the nave) to avoid confusion in studying/recording features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read the façade as a scripted Scripture history in Christ's perspective
rubrics_metrics.description: The order of the attendant powers may be best understood by thinking of them as placed on Christ's right and left hand: this being also the order which the builder adopts in his Scripture history on the façade--so that it is to be read from left to right--i.e. from Christ's left to Christ's right, as He sees it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To interpret sculptural programs, read figures in the sequence intended by the builder (Christ as central corner-stone; prophets and apostles arrayed on His right and left). Understanding the ordered narrative reveals theological meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare original and restored sculpture to judge 'restoration'
rubrics_metrics.description: But in the porches nearly all,--except the actual outside facing, with its rose moulding, of which only a few flowers have been spared here and there. ... the sculpture has been carefully and honourably kept and restored to its place--pedestals or niches restored here and there with clay; or some which you see white and crude, re-carved entirely; nevertheless the impression you may receive from the whole is still what the builder meant; ... Compare its roses with the new ones running round the arches above--and you will know what 'Restoration' means.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for differences of material, carving quality, and finish (e.g., old rose moulding vs. new re-carved flowers) to assess authenticity and the character of restorations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical craftsmanship indicators (joinery, morticing, lightness & order)
rubrics_metrics.description: No nails are used,--all is morticed, and so beautifully that the joints have not moved to this day, and are still almost imperceptible. The four terminal pyramids 'you might take for giant pines ... they are marvels of order and system in construction, uniting all the lightness, strength, and grace of the most renowned spires in the last epoch of the Middle ages.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess quality by construction technique (e.g., morticed joints, absence of nails), precision of fitting, and the unity of lightness, strength and formal grace in structural elements such as spires/pyramids.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary sculpture should avoid pathos; heroes without exultation
rubrics_metrics.description: There is, advisedly, no pathos allowed in primary sculpture. Its heroes conquer without exultation, and die without sorrow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a stylistic principle for evaluating or producing sculpture: ideal primary or foundational sculpture should be restrained in emotion—heroism and death expressed without theatrical pathos.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use symbolic/significatory elements (labyrinth, lion, lamb) to read moral intent
rubrics_metrics.description: The labyrinth ... was an emblem of noble human life--strait-gated, narrow-walled, with infinite darknesses ... to the schools of craftsmen the sign meant further their craft's noblesse, and pure descent from the divinely-terrestrial skill of Dædalus ... The perfect duty of a Bishop is expressed in these six Latin lines--beginning with his pastoral office--Feed my sheep--qui pavit populum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret emblematic devices (labyrinth, animals, floral symbols) for their moral/theological messages; captions and inscriptions are integral to understanding the intended virtues and duties expressed by monument and sculpture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promise-keeping and respectful behavior toward custodians
rubrics_metrics.description: Promise the custode to come back to see it properly; (only then mind you keep the promise;)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respect local custodial expectations (e.g., return visits) as part of proper conduct in sacred/heritage sites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scale comprehension via comparative measurement and analogy
rubrics_metrics.description: From the pavement to the keystone of its vault is but 132 French feet--about 150 English. Think only--you who have been in Switzerland,--the Staubbach falls nine hundred! ... Yet it is twice the height of Amiens' apse!--and it takes good building ... to make your work stand half that height, for six hundred years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use comparative measures and analogies to appreciate engineering achievement and scale (comparing apse height to cliffs or waterfalls gives perspective on construction difficulty and permanence).
